author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels of the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's pulmonary and systemic circuits.
Differentiate the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain functional differences between the right and left heart.
Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker myocardium than the right ventricle based on required pump pressure.
Describe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent backflow and identify which valves separate which chambers or vessel pairs.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1 — Exterior orientation: paired intact and cutaway hearts
modules.description: Introductory exterior view showing a full-size intact heart and a synchronized cutaway heart side-by-side for anatomical orientation and patient vs. viewer perspective.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe anatomical orientation of the heart and explain why left/right are referenced from the patient's perspective.
Locate major external vessels (SVC, IVC, pulmonary trunk/arteries, pulmonary veins, aorta) on the intact heart.
instructions: Use one-finger drag to rotate both heart models together. Tap the 'orientation label' to toggle patient-view overlay.

components.text:
Patient's left/right vs. viewer's left/right
(Tap to toggle overlay)

clips.changeMeaning: Spawn both intact and cutaway heart models and show orientation label so students can see the paired models and patient perspective.
clips.narration: Welcome. On the left is an intact heart showing external vessels. On the right is a cutaway showing internal chambers and valves. Note that anatomical left and right are described from the patient's perspective.

clips.changeMeaning: Increase rotation speed of both heart models so students can inspect external landmarks and correlate the cutaway interior to external features.
clips.narration: Rotate the models to inspect major external landmarks: the superior and inferior venae cavae, the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins returning to the left atrium, and the aorta exiting from the left ventricle.

modules.description: Stepwise highlighting and labeling of the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels using the cutaway model, while corresponding exterior regions on the intact heart are highlighted.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the four chambers and the four valves by name and location.
Map interior structures from the cutaway to external landmarks on the intact heart.
instructions: Watch each label appear in sequence. Use Next/Previous to move through the structural tour.

clips.changeMeaning: Prepare the tour by ensuring both cutaway and intact tour models are visible and ready for sequential highlighting.
clips.narration: We'll tour the major internal structures using the cutaway. Each label will appear in sequence while the same external region on the intact model is highlighted for mapping.

clips.changeMeaning: Show labels for right atrium and right ventricle on the cutaway model so students identify the right-side chambers first.
clips.narration: First, the right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the systemic veins; the right ventricle pumps it to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Hide right-side labels and display left atrium and left ventricle labels to complete chamber identification.
clips.narration: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs, and the left ventricle supplies blood to the systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: Display tricuspid and pulmonary valve labels on the cutaway so students see valve locations relative to chambers.
clips.narration: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle. The pulmonary semilunar valve guards the outflow to the pulmonary trunk.

clips.changeMeaning: Show mitral and aortic valve labels and enable vessel label on intact model so students can map valves to external exits/entries.
clips.narration: The mitral (bicuspid) valve separates the left atrium and left ventricle. The aortic valve opens into the aorta. Note: mitral and bicuspid are interchangeable terms.

modules.description: Color-coded steady-state flows appear in chambers and vessels: blue for deoxygenated, red for oxygenated. Pulmonary and systemic circuits are labeled and briefly highlighted.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Differentiate pulmonary vs systemic circuits by color and path.
Reinforce which side of the heart carries oxygenated vs deoxygenated blood.
instructions: Observe continuous flow coloring; use Next to highlight pulmonary then systemic circuits.

clips.changeMeaning: Enable blue and red flow overlays to indicate deoxygenated and oxygenated blood in the heart chambers and major vessels.
clips.narration: Blue indicates deoxygenated blood on the right heart and pulmonary arteries. Red shows oxygenated blood on the left heart and systemic arteries.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the pulmonary circuit label while dimming the systemic label so students can focus on the lungs loop first.
clips.narration: Now highlighting the pulmonary circuit: right ventricle → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium. Observe the blue-to-red transition in the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Switch emphasis to the systemic circuit label to show the left heart pumping oxygenated blood to the body via the aorta.
clips.narration: Now the systemic circuit: left ventricle → aorta → body capillaries → systemic veins → right atrium. This requires higher pressure and greater myocardium thickness.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4 — Red blood cell step-by-step trace (interactive)
modules.description: A single enlarged red blood cell is traced stepwise through the full dual circulation path. Students press Next to advance the cell one step at a time and hear narration describing each action.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the exact sequential path of a unit of blood through chambers, valves, and vessels.
Observe oxygenation change at the pulmonary capillary step.
instructions: Tap Next to advance the red blood cell to the next anatomical location. Use Previous to step backward. Replay as desired.

components.sciptDescription: Moves a selectable object along a predefined list of path points; supports stepwise advance and reverse via UI controls.

components.text: Red blood cell trace: starting at SVC
Starting: Superior Vena Cava → Right Atrium

clips.changeMeaning: Place the red blood cell at the superior vena cava starting point and initialize the stepper controls and label for interactive tracing.
clips.narration: A red blood cell begins its journey in the superior vena cava, returning deoxygenated blood from the upper body into the right atrium.

components.text: Right Atrium contracts → through Tricuspid valve

clips.changeMeaning: Move the RBC into the right atrium region and update the on-screen label describing the contraction and passage through the tricuspid valve.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

components.text: Right Ventricle → Pulmonary valve → Pulmonary trunk

clips.changeMeaning: Advance the RBC into the right ventricle and then toward the pulmonary outflow path while updating the descriptive label.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts, sending the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries toward the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Move the RBC to the lung capillary region and change its color from blue (deoxygenated) to red (oxygenated) to visualize gas exchange.
clips.narration: In the pulmonary capillaries the cell picks up oxygen — note the color change from blue to red to represent oxygenation.

components.text: Pulmonary veins → Left Atrium → Mitral valve → Left Ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Advance the RBC back to the left atrium through pulmonary veins and toward the left ventricle via the mitral valve with updated label.
clips.narration: Oxygenated blood returns through pulmonary veins to the left atrium, then passes through the mitral valve to the left ventricle.

components.text: Left Ventricle contracts → Aortic valve → Aorta → Body

clips.changeMeaning: Move the RBC into the aortic outflow region to represent systemic ejection from the left ventricle and update the label.
clips.narration: The left ventricle contracts, pushing the oxygenated cell through the aortic valve into the aorta and systemic circulation.

components.text: Systemic veins return deoxygenated blood → SVC (cycle complete)

clips.changeMeaning: Return the RBC to the superior vena cava and revert color to blue to complete the circulation loop and allow replay.
clips.narration: After delivering oxygen to the body, the cell becomes deoxygenated and returns via systemic veins to the superior vena cava, completing the circuit.

modules.description: Side-by-side cross-section models show the thin right ventricular myocardium versus the thick left ventricular myocardium with scale markers and labels to illustrate approximate thickness values.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Quantify and visually compare right and left ventricular wall thicknesses.
Explain why left ventricular thickness is greater due to higher systemic pressure demand.
instructions: Rotate cross-sections to compare walls; inspect scale markers indicating millimeter measurements.

clips.changeMeaning: Show both ventricular cross-sections side-by-side so students can compare wall thicknesses visually.
clips.narration: Here are horizontal cross-sections through both ventricles at the same level to allow direct comparison of wall thickness.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the right ventricular myocardium label and enable a small scale marker to indicate the thin wall measurement.
clips.narration: The right ventricle normally has a thin myocardium (approximately three to five millimeters) because it pumps into the low-pressure pulmonary circuit.

clips.changeMeaning: Hide the right label and display the left ventricular thickness label and a larger scale marker to emphasize the greater thickness.
clips.narration: The left ventricle has a substantially thicker wall (about ten to fifteen millimeters) to generate the higher pressures needed for systemic perfusion.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6 — Valve function and prevention of backflow
modules.description: Demonstrate AV (tricuspid, mitral) and semilunar (pulmonary, aortic) valves in open and closed states. Each valve is shown swapping between an 'open' and 'closed' model to illustrate leaflet behavior.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Differentiate atrioventricular from semilunar valves and identify their locations.
Observe open vs closed valve states and understand how valves prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle.
instructions: Step through each valve's open and closed states using Next/Previous. Observe which valves are open during ventricular contraction vs relaxation.

clips.changeMeaning: Initialize valve models by showing the tricuspid open and pulmonary closed to demonstrate one state and set up transitions.
clips.narration: Valves act as one-way doors. We'll step through open and closed configurations for atrioventricular and semilunar valves to see how they prevent backflow.

clips.changeMeaning: Swap the tricuspid valve from open to closed to visually demonstrate how leaflet apposition prevents blood returning to the atrium during ventricular contraction.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction the tricuspid valve closes to prevent backflow into the right atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Swap pulmonary valve to open state to show how semilunar valves allow forward flow into the pulmonary arteries during systole.
clips.narration: Semilunar valves like the pulmonary valve open during ventricular contraction to allow ejection into the outflow vessels.

clips.changeMeaning: Show mitral valve closed and aortic valve open to illustrate the pattern during ventricular systole on the left side corresponding to right-side behavior.
clips.narration: When the left ventricle contracts the mitral valve is closed while the aortic valve opens — preventing backflow to the atrium and permitting forward flow to the aorta.

modules.description: A formative quiz where the cutaway heart is displayed without labels. The system highlights a structure and presents multiple choice buttons; students select the correct name and hear immediate feedback.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Reinforce recall of chamber, valve, and vessel names and locations.
Provide immediate feedback to correct misconceptions and strengthen identification skills.
instructions: Tap the button corresponding to the correct structure name. Use replay to try the full set again.

components.text: Which structure is highlighted? Choose A/B/C.

clips.changeMeaning: Enable the highlight marker over the current target structure and present multiple-choice buttons with an instruction prompt.
clips.narration: Identify the highlighted structure. Tap the button with the correct name. Immediate feedback will tell you if your choice is correct.

components.text: Correct — that is the left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Update the feedback text to a positive confirmation when the student selects the correct option.
clips.narration: Correct. The left ventricle is responsible for generating systemic pressure and has the thick myocardium.

components.text: Not quite — review the structure highlighted and try again.

clips.changeMeaning: Provide corrective feedback text when the student selects an incorrect answer and prompt a retry.
clips.narration: That's not correct. Remember to use spatial cues from the cutaway to identify chambers and valves.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8 — Blood flow tracing quiz (sequence questions)
modules.description: Interactive sequencing quiz that asks students to choose the next structure in the flow path from multiple options; correct answers advance the sequence.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Test ability to select the next anatomical structure in the blood flow path.
Challenge distinctions such as pulmonary artery vs pulmonary vein and their oxygenation states.
instructions: Read the prompt, then tap the button for the next structure. Correct answers advance the tracing sequence.

components.text: A unit of blood has just entered the right atrium. What is the next structure?
Select the next structure in the path.

clips.changeMeaning: Display the tracing prompt and present three answer buttons to let the student select the next structure in the circulation sequence.
clips.narration: Start the flow tracing quiz. Choose the next structure in the path from the options shown. Correct answers will advance the sequence.

components.text: Correct — proceed to the next step.

clips.changeMeaning: Provide confirmation text when the student selects the correct next structure so they can continue to the following trace step.
clips.narration: Correct. The next structure after the right atrium is the tricuspid valve, allowing flow into the right ventricle.

components.text: Incorrect — recall that pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Provide corrective feedback text for incorrect responses, reminding students of pulmonary and systemic artery/vein oxygenation differences.
clips.narration: That's incorrect. Remember that pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

modules.description: A concise review that highlights the five major concept areas covered in the lab with on-screen summary text and quick highlights of the relevant model regions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Consolidate the lab's major takeaways: structural inventory, dual circuits, flow path, ventricular thickness asymmetry, and valve function.
instructions: Listen to the summary narration; tap any highlighted item to return to that scene for review.

components.text:
Summary:
1) Structural inventory
2) Pulmonary & Systemic circuits
3) Full blood path
4) LV > RV wall thickness
5) Valve function

clips.changeMeaning: Display the recap text panel and prepare the paired recap models for final highlighting of the five major concept areas.
clips.narration: Let's recap the five key areas from this lab: structure, dual circuits, blood path, ventricular thickness, and valve function.

clips.changeMeaning: Rotate both recap models slowly while narration cycles through each concept to reinforce mapping of internal to external structures.
clips.narration: Refer to the recap panel while you rotate the models to mentally map the structural inventory to the function described.
